intro: The finale of Beethoven’s Appassionata Sonata, Op. 57, moves in almost continuous semiquavers. Artur Schnabel plays Beethoven’s long repeat of the development and recapitulation before the faster closing Presto.

sections.label: Intro · Thirteen repeated chords
sections.mNote: The finale begins on the Andante’s diminished seventh chord.

sections.label: A · Running semiquavers in F minor
sections.mNote: The hands exchange a theme in continuous semiquavers.

sections.label: Dev · The tune leaves F minor
sections.mNote: Broken chords begin softly in B♭ minor

sections.label: A′ · F minor returns
sections.mNote: The bass plays F beneath the running tune.

sections.label: Dev · Development, repeated
sections.mNote: The repeat returns to B♭ minor.

sections.label: A′ · Second return of opening theme
sections.mNote: F minor; leads to the Presto.

sections.label: Coda · Presto, short chords then semiquavers
sections.mNote: Short chordal phrases precede the final run of semiquavers.

cues.title: Opening diminished seventh chords
cues.text: The diminished seventh left unresolved at the end of the Andante returns, struck thirteen times. The right hand then begins a semiquaver figure that descends the keyboard towards F minor.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, movement III, bars 1–19, transcribed by Stelios Samelis for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=937 . The thirteen chords are also counted in the Tonic Chord analysis: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First subject in F minor
cues.text: The main theme starts pianissimo over a low F. It rises through the minor chord and runs down again, eight semiquavers to a bar. The left hand soon takes over the semiquavers, and the right hand plays a melody above them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 20–35: F-minor first subject, pianissimo, followed by the exchange between the hands.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second subject in C minor
cues.text: The second subject enters in C minor at bar 76, over continuing semiquavers. Rests break the right-hand phrases, and the left hand plays chords beneath them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 76–96: C-minor second subject, broken right-hand phrases and left-hand chords.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Development, bars 118–158
cues.text: The development begins over a low B♭. The opening theme appears in B♭ minor and then modulates. A new chordal phrase enters at bar 142.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 118–158: B♭-minor opening of the development and new phrase from bar 142.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Walk to Döbling, Ries’s account
cues.text: On a walk to Döbling, ending at eight in the evening, Beethoven hummed and howled the whole way. “A theme for the last Allegro of the sonata has come to me,” he told his pupil Ries. Indoors, hat still on, he raged at the piano for at least an hour.
cues.evidence: Wegeler and Ries, Biographische Notizen über Ludwig van Beethoven (Koblenz, 1838), Ries’s section: the walk to Döbling and the “letzten Allegro der Sonate (in F moll Opus 57)”. Text: https://archive.org/stream/biographischenot00wege/biographischenot00wege_djvu.txt

cues.title: Return of the first subject
cues.text: After a dominant pedal on C in the bass, a low F brings back the opening tune, pianissimo and still running. The second subject also returns in F minor.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 206–228 and 268–288: dominant pedal, returning first subject and second subject in F minor.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Schnabel’s Beethoven cycles, Berlin, 1927 and 1933
cues.text: In January and February 1927, Schnabel played all thirty-two Beethoven sonatas at Berlin’s Volksbühne. He gave the complete cycle again at the Philharmonie in 1933, the year of this recording.
cues.evidence: Schnabel Music Foundation biography, Berlin cycles of 1927 and January–April 1933: https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/

cues.title: Repeat of development and recapitulation
cues.text: The music returns to the low B♭. Beethoven repeats the whole development and recapitulation, so the changing keys and the return to F minor are played a second time. The exposition has no repeat.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition: repeat from the first ending, bars 300–307, to bar 118. The performed second occurrence is aligned to this recording.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First edition and nickname
cues.text: The first edition, dedicated to Count Franz von Brunsvik, came out in Vienna in 1807 from the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. It does not use the name “Appassionata”. The nickname first appeared in 1838, on a four-hand arrangement published by Cranz of Hamburg.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn work page for Op. 57 (dedication, first edition by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, plate 521; “Sonata appassionata” first on the Cranz four-hand edition of 1838): https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/ag9iZWV0aG92ZW4tdml1cjNyEQsSBHdvcmsYgICA7NW9swkM/Sonata+for+piano+%26%23040%3BF+minor%26%23041%3B+op.+57?fromArchive=6299845270700032 . Henle Urtext note: https://www.henle.de/en/Piano-Sonata-no.-23-f-minor-op.-57-Appassionata/HN-58

cues.title: Presto, new theme in F minor
cues.text: Presto. A short chordal theme enters in F minor over a leaping bass, with clipped replies. Beethoven repeats each of its two halves before the semiquavers return.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, printed bars 316–335: Presto and two repeated phrases with alternative endings.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Closing bars in F minor
cues.text: The opening theme returns at the faster tempo. Its semiquavers move downwards to the final chords in F minor, the key of the sonata’s first phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, printed bars 355–371: return of the first subject and F-minor close. Bar numbering includes the written alternative endings.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From opening run to main theme
transitions.to: A · Running semiquavers in F minor
transitions.how: The opening diminished seventh breaks into a descending run. Repeated figures continue over C, the dominant of F minor, and diminish. At the main tune, marked pianissimo, the bass drops to F and the right hand rises through the minor chord.

transitions.title: The bass turns towards B♭
transitions.from: A · Running semiquavers in F minor
transitions.to: Dev · The tune leaves F minor
transitions.how: The C-minor close runs into a descending link. Its final figures turn around A♮, the leading note of B♭, and diminish. The development opens pianissimo on a low B♭, with the first tune recast in B♭ minor above it. A repeat sign marks the beginning of this passage.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 108–122: descending link, diminished figures and B♭-minor development.

transitions.title: The bass returns to F
transitions.from: Dev · The tune leaves F minor
transitions.how: The development ends over a six-bar pedal on C. A rest follows the last dominant chord, and the first theme returns pianissimo over low F. The hands resume their exchanges. Later the second theme returns in F minor (bars 268–288).
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 206–228; second subject in F minor, bars 268–288.

transitions.title: First ending and return to development
transitions.how: The first ending (bars 300–307) sends a run down through both hands. The bass circles A♮ again under a diminuendo. The repeat goes back to bar 118, the low B♭ and pianissimo opening of the development, and the whole recapitulation is then played a second time.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, first ending, bars 300–307, returning to bar 118.

transitions.title: C pedal resolves to F again
transitions.to: A′ · Second return of opening theme
transitions.how: The development is repeated, and bars 206–228 are played a second time. The same six-bar pedal on C returns, and low F again brings back the main theme pianissimo. At the end of this return the pianist takes the second ending at bar 308 and continues into the coda.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, second traversal of bars 206–228, followed later by the second ending at bar 308.

transitions.title: Second ending into the Presto
transitions.from: A′ · Second return of opening theme
transitions.to: Coda · Presto, short chords then semiquavers
transitions.how: The second ending stays in F minor and gets faster, marked sempre più allegro. At Presto an upper chord is held over low F, and then short chordal phrases begin. The left hand plays a springing accompaniment, and each half of the new tune is repeated.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel edition, bars 308–335: second ending, sempre più allegro and Presto.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The selected file’s artist tag, Archive description and Bloesch agree. The session list records a Bechstein piano, without an established serial number.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The original solo-piano finale is identified, but the performing edition and editorial alterations are not documented. Commentary uses the original edition, plate 521. Its repeat of development plus recapitulation is supported by recurring contours in this recording’s analysis; this does not identify Schnabel’s score or establish an edit/take-splice history. The source’s attacca from movement II is distinct from separate-file playback spacing.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Archive’s specific Op. 57 description gives 11.IV.1933, corroborated by the discography and reissue documentation. The general compilation date 1932 is not used for this sonata. The embedded date tag 2001 and repository upload in 2020 do not establish a session or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Abbey Road Studios, Studio No. 3, London, England
fields.note: Bloesch’s work entry identifies Abbey Road Studios, London, and the chronological session list specifies Studio No. 3 and a Bechstein piano.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: His Master’s Voice issued the original recording. The actual pressing or subsequent reissue used to produce the selected MP3 is not identified, so its source-carrier label remains unknown.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The historical complete-sonata issue was HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, part of set DB 2211–2217. That original catalogue is documented, but no source-carrier or reissue catalogue is established for this digital file.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Bloesch assigns the finale to historical sides 2B 6609 and 2B 6610, takes 1; the release-set catalogue lists 2B 6609I and 2B 6610I. Those original issued-side identifiers do not independently establish the take identities, source pressing or side-join location in this MP3.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified for the selected file. Archive uploader recordplayer78 is not assumed to be its engineer or owner. The independently consulted Pristine transfer credits Andrew Rose, but no upstream relationship with this MP3 is documented; that credit is not imported.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added/public on 27 March 2020. Its MP3 carries date tag 2001 without identifying the event or release represented. Neither date is accepted as the analogue-transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The embedded encoder tag states ‘Audiograbber 1.83.01, LAME dll 3.99, 256 Kbit/s, Joint Stereo, Normal quality’.
fields.note: The inspected selected stream contains MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, with an attached JPEG image. Joint-stereo encoding is not evidence of an original stereo session. Analogue equipment, equalisation, restoration, noise reduction, speed/pitch correction and edit history remain unknown. Archive’s inventory calls the file ‘VBR MP3’; that repository label is distinguished from the stream and embedded encoder information.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying Beethoven composition is public domain under the ordinary EU life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The viewable original score supplies historical musical evidence, not clearance of an unidentified modern performing edition. The composition’s term is separate from the recording’s rights.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly states first release in 1934 for HMV DB 2211–2217. Bloesch identifies Op. 57 as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610, distinguishing publication evidence from the 11 April 1933 session. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive Public Domain Mark is not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not adopted. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
